cards.back: A species' role in its ecosystem: habitat, nutrition, interactions and activity pattern. Two species cannot share the same niche in one community.
Two species competing for the same niche cannot stably coexist — the weaker is excluded (Gause's Paramecium experiments).
Fundamental: the full potential range of conditions/resources. Realized: what is actually used after competition and interactions shrink it.

cards.front: Why are invasive species so successful?
cards.back: In a new range they escape their predators, competitors and diseases → rapid population growth → native species displaced.
Structural (body form: blubber, rolled leaves), behavioural (migration, burrowing, nocturnal activity), physiological (internal processes: antifreeze proteins, hibernation metabolism).
The maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely — set by limiting factors (food, water, space, shelter).
Exponential (few individuals, abundant resources, rapid growth) → transitional (slowing as competition rises) → plateau at the carrying capacity.
Density-dependent intensify with density: competition, predation, disease. Density-independent hit regardless: floods, fires, weather.

cards.front: Predator–prey cycle — why does the predator peak lag behind the prey peak?
cards.back: Predators respond to prey abundance with a delay (reproduction takes time): prey rise → predators rise late → prey crash → predators crash → cycle repeats.
Change = (natality + immigration) − (mortality + emigration). All four processes, both arrivals and departures.

cards.front: In situ vs ex situ conservation
cards.back: In situ: protecting species in their habitat (reserves). Ex situ: captive breeding, seed banks, zoos — used together for endangered species.

cards.front: Quadrat sampling — rules for reliable estimates?
cards.back: Random placement (no bias) + enough repeats. Transects sample changes along a gradient instead.
Population ≈ (marked × total second catch) ÷ marked recaptured. Assumes no migration, random mixing, marks don't affect survival.
Sigmoid curves (name the phases + limiting factors), predator–prey graphs (explain the lag), quadrat/Lincoln index calculations — standard shapes.
Detritivore ingests dead matter internally (earthworms, woodlice). Saprotroph secretes enzymes and absorbs externally digested products (fungi, bacteria).
Cause → effect with named mechanisms: e.g. 'more hares → more food for lynxes → lynx population rises (with a delay)'. Never just restate the graph.

cards.front: Growth curve — which phase is which?
cards.back: Exponential (lag-free rapid rise) → transitional (slowing) → plateau at the carrying capacity. Data questions ask you to identify the phase AND its limiting factor.
Species: interbreeding group. Population: all members of one species in an area. Community: all populations of all species in an area.

cards.front: What does a pyramid of energy show?
cards.back: Energy content at each trophic level — always upright, because energy is lost at every transfer (heat from respiration).
